messages.subject: sampling design
parts:
Dear all,

I have to design a monitoring project of a rather elusive bird species,=20
which nests in the pebbly shores of a small Italian river (about 0.6 km=20
large). I think that point counts are recommendable, since these birds are=
=20
very shy and can be detected only using scopes. I would like to avoid any=20
possible disturbance to the nesting birds, thus I think that sampling=20
points should be (systematically) distributed along the river banks. By=20
using this design, however, I have to limit the sampling area in each point=
=20
only to the half-circle toward the river, since this birds do not nest=20
outside the river itself.
I wonder if this design is correct and if it is possible to use Distance to=
=20
plan this survey and calculate coverage probability. Is it possible to=20
force the choice of sampling points only to the boundary of the survey area?

Thank you,


Dimitri

messages.subject: Re: sampling design
parts: > > I have to design a monitoring project of a rather elusive bird species,
> > which nests in the pebbly shores of a small Italian river (about 0.6 km
> > large). I think that point counts are recommendable, since these birds are
> > very shy and can be detected only using scopes. I would like to avoid any
> > possible disturbance to the nesting birds, thus I think that sampling
> > points should be (systematically) distributed along the river banks. By
> > using this design, however, I have to limit the sampling area in each point
> > only to the half-circle toward the river, since this birds do not nest

> > outside the river itself.

This is easily accommodated, by setting the effort for each point to one
half per visit, rather than 1 per visit, or by defining a multiplier, set
equal to one half, BUT ...
> > I wonder if this design is correct and if it is possible to use Distance to
> > plan this survey and calculate coverage probability. Is it possible to
> > force the choice of sampling points only to the boundary of the survey area?

this means that you would be estimating density at (or near) the edge of
the survey area, so the method will underestimate abundance. (The
assumption that points end up at locations with representative densities,
ensured through random or systematic point placement, is violated by this
design.)

Steve Buckland
